modalities.name: The Hands Behind It
modalities.tagline: Sense one ordinary object closely, then wish its makers well.
modalities.whatItIs: A short solo practice that joins close sensing with goodwill. You take one everyday object, such as a mug, an apple or a wool scarf, explore it slowly through touch, sight and smell, and let each detail point you toward the unseen people who grew, made or carried it. Each of them gets a brief silent wish.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill toward strangers can feel abstract, but a real object in your hands is evidence of real people, so letting the senses lead the wish is meant to make kindness toward unknown others feel grounded and specific.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting alone for about 10 minutes, you hold the object and spend a minute or two on each sense in a set order, touch, then sight, then smell, noticing one plain detail each time, such as the ridge where a handle joins a cup. After each detail you loosely picture someone whose work it reflects, a potter, a picker or a driver, and silently offer one wish, such as 'may your day be easy', before returning to the object. You end by simply holding it for a minute.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find loving-kindness phrases hard to mean when the person is only imagined, and anyone who likes quiet, hands-on practices they can do at a kitchen table.
modalities.cautions: It is gentle, but wishing others well can sometimes stir sadness or a sense of distance, so keep sessions short and stop if it feels heavy. It is a self-care practice, not a substitute for professional help with persistent low mood or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: New concept: pick up an everyday thing, a mug or an apple, and explore it slowly by touch, sight and smell. Each detail points to someone who made, grew or carried it, so you send them a quiet wish. Ten minutes, alone, at the kitchen table.

modalities.name: A Tune That Wishes
modalities.tagline: Set one kind wish for someone to a short, simple melody.
modalities.whatItIs: A practice in which you turn a goodwill wish for one person into a four-line tune you can hum or sing. A music teacher or music therapist helps you shape it at first, and after that you sing it to yourself each day and may one day share it with the person.
modalities.coreIdea: Melody may carry warmth that plain phrases lack and makes words easy to remember, so singing a wish is meant to help goodwill feel felt rather than recited, while the long outbreath of singing keeps the body settled.
modalities.whatYouDo: In one or two 45-minute sessions with a music teacher or music therapist, you choose a person, write four short lines of wishes for them, such as 'may your mornings be gentle', and find a simple tune for them on a keyboard or by voice. For about two weeks you then sing or hum it quietly once or twice a day, picturing the person, and notice how the feeling changes as the tune becomes familiar. Sharing it, as a recording or in person, is optional and only if it feels right.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who connect with music more easily than with silent meditation, and anyone who wants a personal, lasting way to hold someone in mind.
modalities.cautions: A song for someone you have lost or are estranged from can bring up grief, so start with someone easy and pause if it becomes heavy. Keep any listening volume moderate, and treat it as a complement to, not a replacement for, professional care when low mood persists.
modalities.tweet: What if a kind wish had a melody? This idea: write four short lines wishing someone well, find a simple tune with a music teacher, then hum it to yourself each day. A song meant to make goodwill feel felt, not recited. Sharing it is optional.

modalities.name: Care in the Lead
modalities.tagline: Easy partner dancing where good leading means your partner feels looked after.
modalities.whatItIs: A small partner dance class in which the steps stay easy and the real skill is care. The person leading treats each signal, pause and turn as a chance to keep their partner comfortable and unhurried, and roles swap often so everyone both gives and receives that care.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill is usually practiced as silent wishes; here it is practiced in how you guide another body, and feeling cared for in return is meant to make kindness something both partners can sense directly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people meet weekly for 60 minutes with a dance teacher, warm up, and learn two or three basic steps of a slow partner dance to gentle music. In each song one partner leads, aiming only for the other's ease, with clear signals, no rushing and a pause if anything feels off, and at the end the follower names one moment that felt looked after. Partners swap roles every song and rotate every few songs, always by mutual agreement.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to practice kindness in a sociable, active way, and dancers who feel tense or judged in partner classes and would like a gentler setting.
modalities.cautions: Partner touch is always optional and agreed each time: anyone can choose a hand-hold only, dance at a distance or sit out, and the teacher keeps a clear floor with room to move. Wear supportive shoes on a non-slip floor, and if you have joint or balance problems, check with a doctor and keep turns small.
modalities.tweet: An idea for a partner dance class: the steps stay easy, and the only measure of good leading is how looked-after your partner feels. Roles swap every song, and touch is always optional. Kindness you practice with your hands and feet.

modalities.name: Beginnings, Endings, Gaps
modalities.tagline: Steady attention on the breath, with one question changing each week.
modalities.whatItIs: A structured three-week sitting course that keeps attention on one object, the breath at the nostrils, so concentration can grow, while asking a different, narrow insight question each week. Week one looks at how each breath sensation starts, week two at how it ends, and week three at the gaps between.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration and insight are often taught as separate stages; here one steady object supplies the calm, and a single narrow question is meant to keep that calm curious rather than drowsy or dreamy.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a first lesson with a meditation teacher, you sit alone each day for 30 minutes: 15 minutes simply resting on the breath at the nostrils, then 15 minutes on the same spot but watching only for the week's feature. If attention drifts, you return to the breath first and the question second, and a weekly check-in with the teacher reviews what you noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who want both a calmer mind and clearer seeing, and who like a clear plan with one thing to look for at a time.
modalities.cautions: Long or intensive sitting can bring up fear, unusual body sensations or altered perception, so build up gradually, keep the freedom to stop and work with a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties. Anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before taking it further or onto a retreat.
modalities.tweet: A new concept for meditators: three weeks on one spot, the breath at the nostrils. The calm stays the same, but the question changes: week one, how sensations begin; week two, how they end; week three, the gaps. Learn it with an experienced teacher.

modalities.name: The Dot on the Wall
modalities.tagline: Moderate cycling intervals with your gaze resting on one small dot.
modalities.whatItIs: An interval session on a stationary bike in which the challenge is attention, not maximum effort. During each moderately hard bout your gaze and mind rest on one small dot on the wall, and over the weeks the bouts grow longer while the effort stays at a level where you breathe hard but are not flat out.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration is usually trained in a calm body, but a rising heart rate and heavy breathing pull attention around, so keeping one steady object through moderate effort is meant to rehearse staying gathered while activated.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, alone, you warm up for 10 minutes, then do 6 bouts of 2 minutes at a moderately hard effort with 2 minutes of easy pedaling between, looking at a dot of tape at eye level. When gaze or attention slides away, you click a small hand counter and come back, and in each recovery you close your eyes and follow the breath until it slows. Once your count falls over a few sessions, you add 30 seconds to each bout rather than more resistance.
modalities.whoItsFor: Exercisers who want their training to double as attention practice, and meditators who would like to test their focus under effort.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart, blood pressure or other medical conditions, warm up, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Keep the bouts moderate rather than all-out, and if concentration practice ever brings strong unusual sensations, ease off and talk to an experienced meditation teacher.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: moderate bike intervals where your eyes and mind rest on one small dot on the wall. Count each time attention slips, and lengthen the bouts as the count falls, not the resistance. Doctor check first; stop for chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: Everyone Watches the Disc
modalities.tagline: A relaxed disc game where every player's eyes stay on the disc.
modalities.whatItIs: A walking-pace passing game for a small group in which the shared aim is one-pointed attention. Whether or not you are near the play, you keep your eyes on the disc at all times, and at random moments a caller shouts 'where?' and everyone points to it.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration is usually a private skill, but a single moving object that the whole group must track turns steady attention into something shared and visible, and laughing at lapses together is meant to keep it light rather than strained.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to fourteen people meet in a park for about an hour, warm up with an easy jog, and pass a disc at a walking or gentle jogging pace on a small field in rounds of 8 minutes with rests between. A rotating caller shouts 'where?' a few times per round, and the group tracks how many calls in a row everyone points correctly, with anyone who was late simply laughing it off. Each round ends with a quick circle where people say when their attention wandered most.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy casual team games but notice their minds drifting during them, and groups who want a playful, outdoor way to practice focus together.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, warm up, keep the pace easy, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Play on even grass, watch for collisions when eyes are on the disc, and stop playing after any knock to the head.
modalities.tweet: A new idea for park games: a slow disc game where everyone, even players far from the play, keeps their eyes on the disc. Someone shouts 'where?' and the whole group points. Focus as a team sport, at an easy pace, with plenty of laughs at the misses.

modalities.name: The Pleasant Pace
modalities.tagline: A steady jog paced to keep one pleasant sensation going.
modalities.whatItIs: An easy, steady walk or jog in which you choose one pleasant sensation of moving, such as the rhythm of your feet or warmth in your legs, and make it your single object of attention. Your pace is set by that sensation: if it fades into strain, you slow down until it returns.
modalities.coreIdea: Some concentration traditions build on pleasant feeling because it holds attention without force, and steady aerobic rhythm can produce that kind of feeling, so one pleasant sensation becomes both the focus and the pace guide.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week, alone, you walk for 5 to 10 minutes to warm up, then jog or walk briskly for 20 to 40 minutes on a familiar, safe route. In the first minutes you find one pleasant sensation and return to it whenever the mind wanders, slowing down whenever effort turns it unpleasant. Afterwards you note roughly how many minutes it held.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find running a grind and want a gentler way in, and meditators who would like a moving form of concentration.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart or other medical conditions, warm up, build time gradually and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Choose routes away from traffic with good footing, and if concentration brings strong unusual sensations or mood swings, ease off and talk to an experienced meditation teacher.
modalities.tweet: Picture a run paced by pleasure: pick one pleasant sensation, like the rhythm of your feet, and keep your attention there. If it turns into strain, slow down until it comes back. An untested idea for gentler, steadier running. Doctor check first.

modalities.name: Every Rep the Same
modalities.tagline: Moderate lifts where the goal is ten repetitions that feel identical.
modalities.whatItIs: A strength session at moderate loads in which the measure of success is sameness. You aim to make each repetition of a simple lift feel exactly like the last, in speed, depth and breath, with attention resting on the felt line of the movement.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration grows by returning to the same object again and again, and a repeated lift done with precision gives that object a clear shape, so the effort of strength training is meant to become practice in a steady, gathered mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, after a 10-minute warm-up, you do three exercises with a weight you could lift about 15 times, such as goblet squats, rows and presses, for 3 sets of 10 slow repetitions with 2 minutes of rest. During each set you rest attention on the movement as it is felt and match every repetition to the first. You add weight only after three sessions in a row feel steady from the first repetition to the last.
modalities.whoItsFor: Lifters who want training to feel calmer and more mindful, and meditators who would like a physical, measurable form of concentration practice.
modalities.cautions: Learn the lifts from a coach, keep good form, breathe out on the effort rather than holding your breath, and check with a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, heart or eye problems. Warm up, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Gym idea, untested: moderate weights, and the goal is ten reps that feel exactly the same, in speed, depth and breath. You add load only when the sets feel steady. Strength training as concentration practice. Learn form from a coach first.

modalities.name: Head in Your Lap
modalities.tagline: Steady attention on the weight and warmth of a resting dog.
modalities.whatItIs: A guided session in an animal-assisted program in which a calm therapy dog chooses to rest its head on your lap or beside your hand. The gentle weight and warmth become your single object of attention, while the professional guides the session and watches the dog's comfort.
modalities.coreIdea: A living, pleasant object may hold attention more easily than the breath, and a dog tends to shift when you fidget or tense, so the animal gives honest, gentle feedback about how settled you are.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 40-minute sessions, a professional trained in animal-assisted work and the dog's handler settle you on a low chair or floor cushion, and the dog is invited, never placed, to rest with you. For 10 to 15 minutes you rest attention on the weight and warmth where the dog touches you, returning to it whenever the mind wanders, and if the dog moves away, you carry on with your hand resting where it was. The session ends with a short talk about what helped you settle.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find meditation hard to start alone but relax around animals, and those who want a gentle, supported introduction to concentration.
modalities.cautions: Tell the team about allergies or fear of dogs first; the dog must be free to leave at any time, and sessions are kept short and spaced out, with hygiene rules, to protect its wellbeing and yours. If concentration brings strong unusual sensations or distress, stop and tell the professional.
modalities.tweet: Here is a gentle new idea: let a calm therapy dog be your meditation object. It chooses to rest its head on your lap, and you keep your attention on its weight and warmth. If you tense, it shifts. The dog can leave whenever it likes.

modalities.name: The Hundred Lifts
modalities.tagline: One slow qigong arm-raise, repeated a hundred times with the breath.
modalities.whatItIs: A standing practice built from a single slow movement: raising the arms with the in-breath and lowering them with the out-breath. You repeat it about a hundred times, letting the unchanging rhythm become the one object of attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration usually rests on a still object, but a single repeated movement offers one that is just as steady and easier to feel, so its sameness is meant to gather attention the way a repeated word can.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the movement from a qigong teacher, you stand alone each morning with feet hip-width apart and knees soft, raise your palms slowly to shoulder height on each in-breath and let them float down on each out-breath, keeping count in tens on your fingers. When attention drifts you notice where it went and return to the feel of the arms and breath, and after ten rounds of ten you stand still for two minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sitting still restless but want a concentration practice, and qigong learners who want to go deeper into one movement.
modalities.cautions: Keep the movement within a comfortable range, sit for it if standing is tiring, and adapt it for shoulder problems. Rarely, intense qigong or concentration practice has been linked to unusual mental or bodily reactions, so build up gradually with a teacher experienced with such difficulties, and anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first.
modalities.tweet: An idea that turns one movement into meditation: raise your arms slowly on each in-breath, lower them on each out-breath, and repeat a hundred times. The sameness is the point. Learn the move from a qigong teacher, then try it at home.

modalities.name: One Topic All Evening
modalities.tagline: A small gathering that keeps returning to a single chosen topic.
modalities.whatItIs: A gathering of a few friends or acquaintances that stays with one topic for the whole conversation, such as 'a place that changed you' or 'what makes a good neighbor'. When talk drifts, anyone can gently bring it back, the way a meditator returns to the breath.
modalities.coreIdea: Conversations usually skip from subject to subject, and staying with one theme asks for the same patient returning that concentration practice uses, which may let talk go deeper and help people listen more fully.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight people meet at someone's home for about 90 minutes, and the host draws one topic from a jar at the start. Everyone talks freely within it, and when the conversation wanders, anyone can ring a small bell or say 'back to the topic'. The evening ends with each person naming one thing someone else said that stayed with them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tire of small talk and want more focused, meaningful conversation, and friends looking for an easy, regular format for getting together.
modalities.cautions: Choose topics everyone is comfortable with and let people pass, because a deeper conversation can touch personal or painful ground. If social situations bring intense fear or persistent low mood, talk to a doctor or therapist rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: Here's a new idea for evenings with friends: pick one topic from a jar and stay with it all night. When talk drifts, anyone can ring a little bell and bring it back, like returning to the breath. Then each person names something that stayed with them.

modalities.name: Walk Until It Fades
modalities.tagline: Follow one stream's sound on a slow walk until you lose it.
modalities.whatItIs: A slow walk along a stream or river in which the sound of the water is your single object of attention. You start where it is loudest and walk gently away, keeping attention on the sound as it softens, and turn back when you can no longer hear it.
modalities.coreIdea: A sound that slowly fades asks for ever finer, steadier listening, so following one natural sound to its vanishing point is meant to gather attention gradually while the walk keeps the body gently moving.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone or with a quiet companion, on a safe path beside moving water, you stand for two minutes at the loudest point, then walk slowly away for 20 to 40 minutes, pausing now and then to find the sound again whenever thoughts take over. When you can no longer pick it out, you stand still for a minute in the quiet and walk back, letting attention open to everything around you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel calmer outdoors and want a simple concentration practice without sitting still, and walkers who would like a quiet focus for their walks.
modalities.cautions: Stay on paths, keep a safe distance from banks, check the weather and tell someone your route, since attention on sound can make you less aware of footing. Keep your eyes open and stay alert to traffic, cyclists and other walkers.
modalities.tweet: Riverside walk idea: start where the water is loudest and walk slowly away, keeping your attention on its sound as it softens. When you can't hear it anymore, stand still for a minute, then head back. A new, simple way to focus. Stay on the path.

modalities.name: The Background Sound
modalities.tagline: Rest attention on a steady hum you usually tune out.
modalities.whatItIs: A short sitting practice that uses an ordinary background sound, such as a fridge hum, a fan or steady rain, as its single object. Instead of shutting noise out, you choose the sound that is always there and let attention settle on it.
modalities.coreIdea: Sounds we normally filter out tend to be steady, neutral and always available, which may make them a dependable concentration object for people who find the breath frustrating.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sitting comfortably for 15 to 25 minutes, you spend the first minute listening widely and then choose the steadiest sound in the room. You keep attention on its texture, pitch and loudness, returning gently each time you drift, and if the sound stops, you rest in the quiet for a minute before opening your eyes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find the breath an uncomfortable or tricky meditation focus, and those who live in noisy places and want a different relationship with sound.
modalities.cautions: If attention to sound brings heightened sensitivity, fear or distress, open your eyes, move and stop for the day, and talk to a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties if it persists. Anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before longer or intensive concentration practice.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: meditate on the fridge hum. Choose the steady background sound you normally tune out, a fan, rain, distant traffic, and rest your attention on it for 15 minutes. Always there and a bit boring, which may be exactly what makes it a steady anchor.

modalities.name: Follow the Bass Line
modalities.tagline: Listen to a whole piece of music following only its bass.
modalities.whatItIs: A listening practice in which you pick one instrument, usually the bass, and follow only that line through a complete piece. When attention jumps to the melody or the vocals, you notice and return to the bass, the way a meditator returns to the breath.
modalities.coreIdea: Music naturally pulls attention toward the tune, so holding to a quieter supporting line asks for steady, chosen focus, while the music itself is meant to keep that focus pleasant.
modalities.whatYouDo: After one or two sessions with a music teacher or music therapist who helps you pick pieces with a clear bass line, you listen alone, eyes closed and at moderate volume, to one piece of 5 to 15 minutes a day. You follow the bass from the first note to the last, then play the same piece once more and listen openly, noticing how it sounds now.
modalities.whoItsFor: Music lovers who want to listen more deeply, and people who find silent meditation hard but focus easily on sound.
modalities.cautions: Keep the volume moderate to protect your hearing, and choose pieces that leave you feeling steady, since sad or intense music can deepen a low mood. Stop if strong emotions become too much, and seek professional support if low mood persists.
modalities.tweet: Try this new idea: play one piece of music and follow only the bass line, start to finish. When your attention jumps to the melody, bring it back. Then play it again and just listen. Concentration practice that still sounds good.

modalities.name: The Full Cup
modalities.tagline: Dance slowly with a cup of water you must not spill.
modalities.whatItIs: A slow group dance in which each person holds a small cup of water and moves to gentle music without spilling it. The cup becomes the single object of attention, and the movement grows larger as concentration steadies.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration usually asks for a still body, but a full cup gives moving attention a clear, honest object, since any lapse shows up as a spill, so the dance is meant to make steady focus playful and visible.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to twelve people meet for 60 minutes with a teacher trained in dance and meditation, warm up, and fill small plastic cups two-thirds full. Over three songs you move with the cup, starting with tiny sways and steps and widening into turns and reaches while attention stays on the cup. You then dance one song without it to feel what has changed, and finish with five minutes of stillness.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a meditative practice that moves and has a gentle challenge built in, and dancers who would like to train focus and control.
modalities.cautions: Use plastic cups, a non-slip floor that is wiped often and plenty of space between dancers, and keep turns small if you have joint or balance problems, since eyes on the cup can make falls more likely. If concentration practice brings strong unusual sensations or distress, stop and talk to the teacher.
modalities.tweet: A playful new concept: dance slowly to gentle music while holding a small cup of water you must not spill. Any lapse in attention shows up straight away, and the moves get bigger as focus steadies. Plastic cups and a non-slip floor, of course.

modalities.name: The Unrepeatable Phrase
modalities.tagline: Repeat one simple dance phrase and notice how each version differs.
modalities.whatItIs: A movement practice in which you repeat one short dance phrase many times, not to perfect it but to notice how every repetition is different. Breath, balance, mood and the feel of the music keep shifting, and the practice is to see that change clearly without correcting it.
modalities.coreIdea: Insight meditation looks at how experience never repeats exactly, and a movement you try to repeat makes that change unusually easy to feel, so the phrase is meant to become a lens on change rather than a goal to get right.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to twelve people meet for 60 minutes with a teacher trained in meditation and dance, warm up, and learn a simple eight-count phrase, such as a step, a reach and a turn. Each person dances it ten times to slow music, and after each repetition stands still for a breath and silently names one thing that was different, such as 'heavier' or 'faster'. The session ends sitting quietly, and partners may share a few observations.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want an active doorway into insight meditation, and dancers who feel stuck on getting moves 'right'.
modalities.cautions: Use a clear, non-slip floor with plenty of space, keep the phrase within your comfortable range of motion and sit out whenever your joints or balance tell you to. Close observation can sometimes bring up unsettling feelings, so stop if it does and talk to an experienced teacher if they persist.
modalities.tweet: For dancers, a new concept: repeat one short phrase ten times and, after each go, notice one thing that was different. Heavier, faster, wobblier. You are not trying to get it right, only to see that no movement ever happens the same way twice.

modalities.name: Build-a-Routine Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard dance intervals that each add one move to a routine.
modalities.whatItIs: An energetic group class built from hard intervals of dancing, in which each bout teaches one new move. By the last bout the moves join into a short routine you have learned while breathing hard, and the class dances it together to finish.
modalities.coreIdea: Intervals usually measure progress only in effort, so attaching one new skill to each bout is meant to give hard work a visible payoff, a dance you can do by the end, which may make it more fun and memorable.
modalities.whatYouDo: Ten to twenty people meet for 45 minutes with an instructor qualified in fitness and dance, warm up for 10 minutes, then do six bouts of 1 to 2 minutes of hard dancing to upbeat music, each teaching a new move, with 1 to 2 minutes of easy walking between. In each bout you repeat the new move plus the ones before it, and the class ends with the full routine at an easier pace and a cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find plain intervals dull and like music and learning, and dancers who want a tougher workout.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart, blood pressure or joint problems, warm up, build up gradually, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Use a sprung or non-slip floor, keep jumps optional, and leave space between dancers to avoid collisions and falls.
modalities.tweet: Interval training, reimagined: each hard bout teaches you one new dance move, and by the last bout they link into a short routine you learned while breathing hard. Easy walking between bouts, jumps optional, doctor check first.

modalities.name: Score When They Nail It
modalities.tagline: Teams invent dance moves and score when rivals perform them well.
modalities.whatItIs: A lively game for two teams in which each side invents a short, energetic dance phrase and teaches it to the other. Points go to the team that taught, based on how well the other side performs it, so winning depends on teaching clearly and cheering rivals on.
modalities.coreIdea: In most sport you win by making the other side fail; here you score only when they succeed, so the energy and belonging of team play are meant to point toward helping each other rather than beating each other.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of five to eight meet in a hall or on grass for about an hour with a volunteer host, warm up together, and have 5 minutes to invent an eight-count phrase full of travelling steps, jumps or turns. Each team then has 3 minutes to teach it, the other team performs it twice to music, and the teaching team scores the performance out of five under a spirit rule of honest, generous calls. Rounds repeat with new phrases, and the game ends with everyone dancing all the phrases together.
modalities.whoItsFor: Groups who like team games but want less aggression, and people who enjoy dancing but feel shy about it alone.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint or other health problems, warm up, keep jumps optional and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Leave space to avoid collisions, use a non-slip floor or even grass, and keep any partner contact in a phrase optional and agreed.
modalities.tweet: What if the only way to score was helping the other team? In this new game, each team invents a short dance move and teaches it to its rivals, and points go to the teachers when the rivals nail it. Team spirit, pointed the other way.

modalities.name: The Dancing Mile
modalities.tagline: A long, steady outing where you travel by dancing instead of running.
modalities.whatItIs: A steady, continuous outing in which you cover a set loop by dancing, with travelling steps, skips, side-steps and grapevines, at an effort you could keep up for half an hour or more. It has the even rhythm of endurance training and the play of dance, and it can be done alone, with a friend or with a small group.
modalities.coreIdea: Steady aerobic effort often feels like a grind, and dance turns the same continuous effort into play, so letting the steps carry you along a route is meant to make long, even exercise something to look forward to.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, you warm up for 10 minutes and then dance-travel around a park loop, a track or a large hall for 20 to 45 minutes to a playlist with a steady, moderate tempo. You keep to a pace where you can still talk in short sentences, change steps whenever you like, and finish with a few minutes of easy walking.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find running boring or hard on the joints but want steady exercise, and dancers who want to build stamina.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart or other medical conditions, warm up, build time gradually and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Choose even, uncrowded ground away from traffic, keep music low enough to hear your surroundings, and spare your knees and ankles with low, light steps.
modalities.tweet: Bored of running? An idea: cover a park loop by dancing instead. Skips, side-steps, grapevines, at a steady pace you could keep up for half an hour. Endurance training that feels like play. Even ground, music low, doctor check first.

modalities.name: Floor and Back Up
modalities.tagline: Slow dance phrases of lowering to the floor and rising again.
modalities.whatItIs: A strength class built from dance floor work: slow, controlled phrases that take you down to the floor and back up to standing in different ways. As you get stronger, the phrases slow down and use less help from the hands, which is how the load increases.
modalities.coreIdea: Getting down to the floor and up again with control is a strength skill that matters in daily life, and making it a dance phrase is meant to turn resistance training into graceful, expressive movement with clear, step-by-step progression.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people meet twice a week for 60 minutes with an instructor trained in dance and strength training, warm up, and learn three or four phrases set to slow music, such as a lunge that lowers to kneeling, a roll to sitting and a rise through a squat. Each phrase is repeated for 3 sets of about 6 slow repetitions with rests between. Progress comes from slowing the count, using fewer hand touches or holding a light weight.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want strength training that feels like dance, and anyone who wants more confidence getting down to the floor and back up.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart, blood pressure, knee, hip or back problems, warm up, use mats on a non-slip floor and keep hand support available, since falls are the main risk. Breathe steadily through the slow rises rather than holding your breath, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Strength training made of dance floor work, as a new concept: slow phrases take you from standing down to the floor and back up, and you progress by slowing the count and using less help from your hands. Mats, a doctor check and no rushing.

modalities.name: Moving Like the Herd
modalities.tagline: Watch a horse herd, then move together as a human herd.
modalities.whatItIs: A guided group session at a stable or farm in which people first watch a herd of horses moving together in their paddock, then try moving as a human herd in a nearby arena. A professional trained in animal-assisted work and a dance movement therapist lead it together, and the horses stay free and are never asked to perform.
modalities.coreIdea: Herds coordinate without words through spacing, following and noticing each other's comfort, so borrowing those patterns is meant to help a group sense personal space and move together with attention and respect.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to ten people meet for 90 minutes and spend about 20 minutes watching the horses from outside the fence, while the animal professional points out how they keep their distance, follow and change leaders. In the arena the group then practices those patterns in silent movement to soft music, such as drifting as one, letting a new leader emerge and showing with the body when someone is too close. The session ends with a talk about what people noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to sense or set personal space with others, and groups who would enjoy a calm, outdoor way of moving together.
modalities.cautions: The horses are watched from outside the fence, never chased or crowded, and the session pauses if they seem stressed; anyone with allergies or fear of horses should say so first, and everyone follows the yard's safety rules. Uneven ground and weather add fall risk, so wear sturdy shoes, keep movements within your range and keep any touch between people optional.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment for a farm visit: watch a herd of horses move together, how they keep space, follow and change leaders, then try moving as a human herd nearby. The horses stay free and are never asked to perform. A group lesson in personal space.

modalities.name: Form, Loosen, Return
modalities.tagline: A set qigong-style sequence that melts into free dance and back.
modalities.whatItIs: A group class that begins with a fixed sequence of slow qigong-style movements, gradually loosens it into free dance, and then gathers the movement back into the same form. The arc from structure to freedom and back is the practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Qigong values a steady, repeatable form and dance values free expression, and moving between them on purpose is meant to show that you can let go of structure and still find your way back to calm.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to fifteen people meet weekly for 60 minutes with a teacher trained in qigong and dance, and do a simple eight-movement sequence slowly with the breath. Over the next 20 minutes, to music that slowly builds, each repetition gets looser, bigger and more personal until it becomes free dancing. Over the final 15 minutes the music softens and everyone returns step by step to the original form, ending in stillness.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like structure but want to loosen up, and dancers who want a calmer, more grounded practice.
modalities.cautions: Use a non-slip floor with enough space, keep movements within a comfortable range and adapt them for joint or balance problems. Rarely, intense qigong practice has been linked to unusual mental reactions in people who were already vulnerable, so anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should check with a doctor first.
modalities.tweet: Start slow and set, end free, then come back. This new class idea opens with a qigong-style form, lets it loosen bit by bit into free dance, then gathers it back into the form and finishes in stillness. Practice in letting go and finding your way back.

modalities.name: Teach Me Your Step
modalities.tagline: A social evening where everyone teaches one step from their life.
modalities.whatItIs: A relaxed social evening where each guest brings one dance step picked up somewhere in life, at a wedding, a school disco, a family party or from a video, and teaches it to one or two others. Pairs rotate, and the stories behind the steps become the conversation.
modalities.coreIdea: Being the teacher for a few minutes gives everyone a clear role and something to offer, and a step's back story is an easy opening for talk, so the evening is meant to turn strangers into acquaintances through small, shared lessons.
modalities.whatYouDo: Ten to thirty people gather in a hall, cafe or home for about two hours with a host and a playlist, and every 10 minutes the host calls for new pairs or trios. In each round one person teaches their step and says where it comes from, the others try it, and then they swap. The evening ends with everyone dancing the steps they collected, followed by snacks and free time to talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to meet others but dislike small talk at mixers, and communities that want a simple, welcoming way to bring neighbors together.
modalities.cautions: Any step at any level is welcome, touch is always optional and agreed, and anyone can watch instead of dancing; keep the floor clear and non-slip. If social situations bring intense fear or persistent low mood, talk to a doctor or therapist rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: Neighborhood night idea: everyone brings one dance step they picked up somewhere, a wedding, a school disco, a grandparent, and teaches it to someone new. Pairs rotate every ten minutes, and the stories behind the steps do the small talk for you.

modalities.name: Dance at the Good Spots
modalities.tagline: A group walk that stops to dance wherever someone feels moved.
modalities.whatItIs: An unhurried group walk in a park, a wood or along a coast where anyone can stop the group at a spot they love and start a short, free dance there. Others join in however they like, and the walk becomes a string of places marked by movement.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving in a place may make it more memorable than only looking at it, and letting anyone choose where to dance keeps the walk open and shared, so the landscape and the group's play are meant to shape each other.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to twelve people meet for a 60 to 120 minute walk on a known, easy route with a host who carries a small speaker or nothing at all. Whenever someone feels drawn to a spot, such as a clearing, a bridge or a patch of sand, they call a stop and dance for a minute or two to music, birdsong or wind, while the group joins, watches or rests. At the end, each person names the spot they will remember.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy walking outdoors and want more play and connection on their walks, and those who feel shy dancing indoors but freer outside.
modalities.cautions: Plan the route, check the weather, tell someone where you are going and choose dancing spots with safe, even footing away from edges, roots and water. Keep music quiet out of respect for wildlife and other people, and keep any touch between people optional.
modalities.tweet: Picture a group walk where anyone can call a stop at a spot they love, a bridge, a clearing, a patch of sand, and start a short dance there. Others join, watch or rest. A new idea that turns the route into a string of places you danced.

modalities.name: Feet First Floors
modalities.tagline: Slow barefoot dancing across changing textures, felt through your feet.
modalities.whatItIs: A slow, barefoot dance practice on a path of different textures, such as grass, sand, smooth wood, a rug and cool tiles. Attention stays on what the soles of the feet feel, and the movement responds to each surface.
modalities.coreIdea: The feet are full of sensation that shoes and habit usually mute, and letting each texture shape how you move is meant to make dancing a way of feeling the present rather than performing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone or with a few friends, in a garden, on a beach or in a room laid out with mats and trays of safe materials, you move slowly to quiet music or none for 20 to 30 minutes. On each surface you pause to feel its temperature, give and grain, then let that feeling shape your steps, softer on sand and gliding on wood, before moving on to the next.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy sensory mindfulness but want to move, and anyone who feels self-conscious dancing and would like a quiet focus that is not about how they look.
modalities.cautions: Check every surface for sharp objects, heat and slipperiness, keep surfaces level, and skip barefoot work if you have reduced feeling in your feet, foot wounds or diabetes affecting the feet. Move slowly with space around you to avoid falls, and stop if heightened sensitivity becomes uncomfortable.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: dance slowly barefoot across grass, sand, smooth wood and cool tiles, letting each texture shape how you move. Softer on sand, gliding on wood. Attention on your soles, not on how you look. Check surfaces for anything sharp first.

modalities.name: Who's Leading Now
modalities.tagline: Dancers and musicians take turns following each other's lead.
modalities.whatItIs: A group session with live percussion and simple instruments in which the lead keeps passing between the people playing and the people dancing. Sometimes the dancers follow the music, and sometimes the players must follow the dancers' movements with their sound.
modalities.coreIdea: Being followed can feel powerful, and following closely asks for real attention, so swapping who leads between sound and movement is meant to turn music and dance into a conversation in which everyone both shapes and responds.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to sixteen people meet for 75 minutes with a facilitator trained in music or dance therapy, warm up, and split into a few players with drums, shakers or a keyboard and a larger group of dancers. In rounds of about 5 minutes the facilitator signals whether sound or movement leads, for example the dancers slowing down and the players having to slow with them, and roles swap so each person both plays and dances. A short sharing circle ends the session.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love music and movement and want a creative, social group, and anyone curious how it feels to lead and to follow without words.
modalities.cautions: Keep instruments at a comfortable volume, give dancers enough non-slip space, and adapt movements for joint or balance problems. Strong feelings can come up in expressive group work, so treat it as a complement to, not a replacement for, professional treatment.
modalities.tweet: What if the band had to follow the dancers? In this new idea the lead keeps switching: sometimes dancers move to the drums, sometimes the drummers must match the dancers. Everyone takes turns at both. Music and movement as a conversation.
